title: Even that is a view
hookLine: a wanderer says "I accept no view"; Sariputta, fanning the Buddha, awakens
carry: noticing the grip of an opinion

cards: A dinner table, and everyone is arguing. One guest leans back and says: I don't have opinions. I'm above all that.
It sounds wise, even humble. In a cave called the Boar's Cave on Vulture Peak, outside the city of Rājagaha, a wanderer named Dīghanakha, Long-Nails, comes to the Buddha and says almost exactly that.
Standing behind the Buddha, fanning him, is Sāriputta. Tradition says he has been a monk for about two weeks. He's only there to keep the air moving.

teach.b: Dīghanakha's words, in paraphrase: nothing is acceptable to me. No view at all. The Buddha's reply is gentle and almost funny.

teach.h: IS THAT VIEW ACCEPTABLE TO YOU?
teach.b: This view of yours, that nothing is acceptable to you: is that view acceptable to you? Long-Nails sees the trap and tries to wriggle: even if it were, it would be the same. But the point has landed.
Saying I hold no views is itself a view, one that can hide behind looking neutral. The Buddha doesn't win the argument and leave.
He describes how views of every kind, everything is acceptable, nothing is, some things are, lead to clinging and quarrel, and how a wise person, seeing that, lets go of the clinging.
Then he turns to the body and to feeling. When you feel a pleasant feeling, you're not feeling a painful one at that moment. Each feeling comes and goes; none is worth grasping as me or mine.
While Sāriputta stood there fanning, the sutta says, he reflected on what he heard, and his mind was freed from clinging. The commentary says Dīghanakha was his nephew.
One man came to argue and left with a first glimpse of the teaching. The other was just moving the air, and woke up. The practice wasn't a better opinion.
It was noticing the grip any opinion can have on us, even the opinion of having none.

how: Buddhist traditions teach letting go of clinging to views, and the story of Sāriputta's awakening while fanning the Buddha is often told on retreats as a sign that insight can come in the middle of ordinary service.

o: a vow to hold no opinions at all
a view, an opinion, a way of seeing
a wise debater who wins arguments

games.q: in the Boar's Cave: tap the pairs.
p: is that view acceptable to you?

s: Sāriputta was freed while debating Dīghanakha himself
he was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him, and reflecting on what he heard.
saying 'I accept no view' can itself be a view
the Buddha's question shows it: is that view acceptable to you?
the commentary says Dīghanakha was Sāriputta's nephew
the sutta doesn't say so; the later commentary does.

games.q: a guest says: I don't accept any views. you're the Buddha. what do you ask?
o: is that view acceptable to you?
games.why: one question shows that even 'no views' is a view, and then the Buddha turns to what all views share: they can be clung to.

practice: Let one strong opinion come to mind, about family, about how people should behave, and notice how tightly it's held. Then look for the opinion behind it, if there is one, maybe that you're the reasonable one, or above it all.
Don't drop it or defend it; just see whether the grip changes on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Ditthi. A wanderer claimed to hold no views, and the Buddha asked if he held that one. Sāriputta, listening, was freed.

orig.note: Pali diṭṭhi (Sanskrit dṛṣṭi): view, opinion, literally a way of seeing.

carryVoice: Your line: noticing the grip of an opinion. Even no views can be held tight. Day four hundred sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: Papañcasūdanī (commentary on MN 74): Dīghanakha as Sāriputta's nephew; Sāriputta's fortnight as a monk
